body.stem: Your team is creating a Backup vault in the Azure portal for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server, and you are on the Instance details tab of the create wizard. Business continuity requires the recovery points to survive the loss of an entire Azure region, and the team must be able to rehearse a regional recovery during planned drills without waiting for an outage declaration. Which storage redundancy setting and companion toggle should you select?

rows: Location of the primary copy of the protected database
Recovery points must remain available if an entire region is lost
Recover from the paired region during scheduled drills while the primary region is healthy
Billing at RA-GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups held in the vault is acceptable
The redundancy value must be settled at creation time and cannot be changed once items are protected

options.text: Geo-redundant (GRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled
Geo-redundant (GRS) only, keeping the paired region sealed until an outage is declared
Zone-redundant (ZRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled
Locally redundant (LRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled

explanation.correct: Geo-redundant (GRS) keeps a second copy of the recovery points in the Azure paired region, which is what protects against loss of an entire primary region; it is also the recommended setting when Azure holds the primary copy of the data. Turning on Cross Region Restore then makes those secondary-region recovery points available for restores and regional resiliency drills at any time, with no outage declared in the primary region. Enabling Cross Region Restore is billed automatically at RA-GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups stored in the vault, which the scenario accepts.

perChoice.b: With Geo-redundant (GRS) alone the backups in the paired region become accessible only after Microsoft declares an outage in the primary region, so the scheduled drill during a healthy primary region cannot be performed. This setting satisfies the regional-outage requirement but not the rehearsal requirement.
perChoice.c: Zone-redundant (ZRS) keeps the redundant copies inside the primary region, spread across availability zones. It does not maintain a copy in the Azure paired region, so it satisfies neither the loss-of-region requirement nor restores from the paired region.
perChoice.d: Locally redundant (LRS) stores copies within the region only and is the recommended choice when Azure is not the primary backup storage endpoint, because it reduces Azure storage cost. It offers no protection against loss of the region and no paired-region recovery points to restore from.

body.stem: You have an Azure Backup vault named prod-vault in the East US region that protects an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server. The vault is protected by a key that your organization keeps in the Azure Key Vault kv-backup-keys, and the only principal listed with a role on that Key Vault is the vault's own identity. Since the last key rotation, every scheduled and on-demand backup job fails with a key retrieval error. You need the backup jobs to succeed again while keeping the key under your own control in Azure Key Vault. Which access change should you make?

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server
prod-vault (System Assigned Managed Identity) - Key Vault Crypto User

options.text: Grant the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.
Grant the Backup Management Service access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.
Grant the vault's User Assigned Managed Identity access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.
Grant the Backup vault resource itself access to the Key Vault so it can read the key.

explanation.correct: When a Backup vault uses Customer Managed Keys, the key read against Azure Key Vault is performed by the Backup Management Service; the vault's managed identity is not the actor that reaches into the Key Vault. The exhibit shows that only the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity holds a role on kv-backup-keys and that jobs still fail with a key retrieval error, so the missing piece is access for the Backup Management Service. Granting that service access to the Key Vault lets the key be used for the vault's encryption while the key stays under your own control.

perChoice.a: The vault's System Assigned Managed Identity already holds Key Vault Crypto User on that Key Vault, and permissions given to a vault's managed identity are not what make Customer Managed Keys work, because the key read is carried out by the Backup Management Service.
perChoice.c: A User Assigned Managed Identity can be attached to a vault and outlives the vault, but it is not the principal that reads the encryption key, so granting it a role on kv-backup-keys leaves the failing jobs unchanged; the Backup Management Service needs the access instead.
perChoice.d: The vault resource itself is not the principal that performs the key read either. Only the Backup Management Service reads the key for Customer Managed Keys, so granting the vault resource access in the Key Vault does not resolve the failures.

body.stem:
You have a Backup vault named fin-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. It protects an Azure Disk named data-finance01, which sits in resource group rg-data. A backup policy runs from an automation account whose run-as identity is svc-backup-runner, and every attempt to back up the disk ends with an authorization error reporting that access to data-finance01 was denied. The access configuration that is in place today is listed below.

You need the disk backups to complete with the smallest possible permission footprint, and the automation account must not receive any write or delete permission on data-finance01. Which change should you make?

options.text: Grant the fin-vault System Assigned Managed Identity the Reader role on the Azure Disk data-finance01.
Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Reader role on the Azure Disk data-finance01.
Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Owner role on the resource group rg-data.
Grant the svc-backup-runner run-as identity the Key Vault Reader role on the Key Vault kv-backup-keys.

explanation.correct: Whoever creates or updates a backup instance must be able to read the source resources, and that grant has to sit with the user or service identity that performs the work rather than with the vault's managed identity. In this scenario svc-backup-runner is the run-as identity that creates and updates the backup instance for the disk, so handing it the Reader role on data-finance01 is the minimal change that removes the authorization error, and Reader grants no write or delete permission on the disk.

perChoice.a: The vault's managed identity is not the party that creates or updates the backup instance. The documentation is explicit that the read grant on the source belongs to the user or service identity doing that work, not to the vault's managed identity, so granting Reader to the fin-vault identity does not clear the denial.
perChoice.c: Owner on rg-data hands the automation account full control over every resource in the group, including write and delete rights on the protected disk, which breaks the requirement to keep the footprint minimal and read-only.
perChoice.d: Key Vault Reader on kv-backup-keys governs access to key material stored in that Key Vault. The protected disk lives in rg-data, so this assignment grants nothing on data-finance01 and the backup continues to be denied.

body.stem: You are creating two Azure Backup vaults in the Contoso-prod subscription — prod-vault in rg-blue and test-vault in rg-green. The platform team wants one managed identity to carry the access grants for prod-vault and for test-vault, so that the grants are administered in a single place. During the Q1 migration, prod-vault will be deleted and re-created, and the identity that carries the grants must still be usable afterwards. Which managed identity configuration should you use?

rows: Resource group rg-blue, region West Europe
Resource group rg-green, region West Europe
Azure RBAC, with the vault's managed identity carrying the grants
A single set, for prod-vault and for test-vault

options.text: System Assigned Managed Identity, created with each vault and removed with that vault
User Assigned Managed Identity, created independently and referenced by both vaults
User Assigned Managed Identity, created once for each vault, so each of the vaults keeps a separate identity
System Assigned Managed Identity, created for one vault and reused by the other vault

explanation.correct: A User Assigned Managed Identity is a standalone object whose lifecycle is separate from the vaults it is attached to: it can be attached to one or several vaults, it can be shared across vaults, and it outlives the deletion or re-creation of a vault. That lets a single identity and a single set of role assignments serve prod-vault and test-vault, and it keeps working after prod-vault is deleted and re-created during the Q1 migration.

perChoice.a: The System Assigned Managed Identity is generated together with the vault and is bound to that vault's lifecycle. Each vault would therefore need its own identity and its own set of grants, and the identity of prod-vault would disappear with the vault during the migration, leaving the grants dangling.
perChoice.c: Creating one identity per vault produces two identity objects and two sets of grants, which does not meet the requirement of a single identity and a single set of role assignments covering prod-vault and test-vault. It also states that the identity is removed with its vault, which is not how a user-assigned identity behaves — such an identity survives deletion and re-creation of the vault it is attached to.
perChoice.d: A System Assigned Managed Identity belongs to the vault that generated it and is bound to that vault's lifecycle, so it cannot be attached to a second vault and cannot be reused by test-vault. It also disappears when prod-vault is deleted, so it would not satisfy the requirement that the grants remain usable after the vault is re-created.

body.stem:
You are retiring the Backup vault pg-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. Every attempt to remove it from the portal is refused, and the vault must be gone by the end of the change window. The state reported for the vault is shown below.

You need the vault removed together with everything it holds, and no backup data may survive in the subscription afterwards. Which change should you make?

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server
Refused - the vault still holds protected items and stored backup data

options.text: Remove all backup policies from the vault but leave the backup instances in place, then delete the vault.
Remove all backup instances and backup policies from the vault, then delete the vault.
Remove all backup instances from the vault but leave the backup policies in place, then delete the vault.
Change the vault's storage redundancy to Locally redundant and detach the vault's managed identity, then delete the vault.

explanation.correct: A vault is refused for deletion while it still holds protected data sources or backup data, and a Backup vault can hold both backup instances and backup policies, so both kinds of object have to go before the vault itself can be removed. This vault still carries the protected items pg-fin-01 and data-disk-01 together with the policies pg-daily-90d and disk-daily-30d, so the correct change is to remove every entry from the Backup Instances view and every remaining backup policy, then delete the vault. When hunting for leftovers, work through each Datasource type filter, because a single instance or policy hidden under one filter value keeps the vault undeletable. Remember that removal cannot be undone: the recovery points of the protected servers disappear permanently, which matches the requirement that no backup data survive the decommission.

perChoice.a: Removing only the backup policies leaves the backup instances and the protected data sources with their recovery points inside the vault. The delete request is still refused while any backup instance or backup data remains, so the operation fails.
perChoice.c: Removing only the backup instances leaves the backup policies in the vault. Both backup instances and backup policies must be gone before the vault can be deleted, so the portal keeps refusing the delete request.
perChoice.d: Neither part of this change releases anything: the redundancy level is in fact locked once items are protected, and detaching the vault's managed identity leaves the protected items and their stored recovery points untouched. The vault therefore stays undeletable.

body.stem:
You have a Backup vault named contoso-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription, and it protects an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server. A separate company runs its own Microsoft Entra tenant, and after a ransomware incident locks the Contoso side out, that company must bring the PostgreSQL server's vaulted backup data into fabrikam-vault, which it owns and administers. The partner must be able to do this without holding any account in the Contoso-prod subscription, and the Contoso team must not expose the stored backup data to partner users.

You need the partner to be able to work with the PostgreSQL server's vaulted backup data through fabrikam-vault. Which change should you make?

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server
fabrikam-vault (owned by the partner, East US)

options.text: Configure Cross Tenant Restore (preview) on contoso-vault and create a mapping from contoso-vault to fabrikam-vault
Configure Cross Region Restore on contoso-vault so the partner can pull the PostgreSQL recovery points from the paired region to a new server

Create and configure a second Geo-redundant Backup vault named fabrikam-vault inside the Contoso-prod subscription, re-protect the PostgreSQL server with it, and add the partner's guest account as Owner on it
Configure a guest account for the partner in the Contoso-prod tenant with Owner on contoso-vault so their administrators can copy the recovery points into fabrikam-vault themselves

explanation.correct: Cross-tenant restore (preview) is the supported way to bring vaulted data from a source vault into a vault that lives in a different tenant: it recovers the vaulted backup data from the source tenant into the target vault by mapping the source Backup vault to that target vault. You configure it on the source vault (contoso-vault) and create the mapping to the partner's vault (fabrikam-vault), after which the protected items and their recovery points can be worked with from fabrikam-vault. The exhibit fits this capability: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server is one of the workloads the preview feature covers, and fabrikam-vault is owned by the partner in a separate tenant, so it can act as the target vault. Ordinary restores stay inside one tenant, so nothing else in the current configuration brings the data across.

perChoice.b: Cross Region Restore only replicates the PostgreSQL backups to the paired Azure region and opens the secondary copy so you can rehearse recovery there; it keeps the data within the same tenant, so it cannot make the protected data available through fabrikam-vault in the partner's tenant.
perChoice.c: A second vault created inside the Contoso-prod subscription remains in the same tenant as the source data, and a guest account on it is still an account in the Contoso-prod subscription. Only the cross-tenant capability brings vaulted data into a vault in another tenant.
perChoice.d: The vaulted backup data is kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, so partner guests have no direct route to that storage even if they are given an Owner role on contoso-vault. Role assignments made inside the Contoso-prod tenant cannot be used to copy the data into fabrikam-vault themselves.

body.stem: You have a new Azure Backup vault named blob-vault that the platform team is creating in the Contoso-prod subscription to hold vaulted backups for an Azure Blob container. The blob data's primary copy is kept on an on-premises NAS appliance outside Azure, finance has capped the vault's monthly storage charge at the cheapest tier the platform team approves, and the stated recovery objective covers restoring in the same Azure region only. You need the vault's storage footprint chosen correctly while the vault is being created so that the monthly charge stays within the approved cap. Which storage redundancy setting should you select?

rows: Location of the workload's primary data copy
Capped at the cheapest tier the platform team approves
Restore within West Europe; no requirement to recover from a regional outage
Items already protected in the vault

options.text: Locally redundant (LRS)
Zone-redundant (ZRS)
Geo-redundant (GRS)
Geo-redundant (GRS) with Cross Region Restore enabled

explanation.correct: Because Azure is not where the primary copy of the backed-up data lives, the documented guidance is to choose Locally redundant (LRS) for the vault, which reduces Azure storage cost. The vault currently holds no protected items, so this is the point at which the setting can still be chosen — once items are protected, a vault's storage redundancy cannot be changed.

perChoice.b: Zone-redundant (ZRS) spreads copies across availability zones and is the costlier option, so it does not match a vault whose approved charge is capped at the cheapest tier, and the recovery objective does not require surviving the loss of an availability zone.
perChoice.c: Geo-redundant (GRS) is the default that Microsoft recommends when Azure itself is the primary backup storage endpoint. In this case the primary copy sits on-premises, so keeping a replicated copy in a paired region adds cost that exceeds the approved cap.
perChoice.d: Cross Region Restore is a companion capability for vaults that use GRS, letting restores run from the paired region, and it carries additional charges (for PostgreSQL backups held in such a vault, billing moves to RA-GRS rates). It is irrelevant to a same-region restore objective and would push the vault above the approved minimum charge.

body.stem:
You have a new Azure Backup vault that the platform team is creating in the Contoso-prod subscription to hold vaulted backups for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server. Contoso's security policy requires that the key protecting the vaulted backup data be generated, stored, rotated and revoked by Contoso's own security team inside Contoso's own Azure Key Vault. The same policy requires that role-based control over backup and restore operations on the vault, including which workloads the vault is allowed to back up, stays enforced. This vault serves a single team and is not shared with any other vault. The configuration decided so far is listed below.

You need the new vault configured so that both parts of the policy hold. Which change should you make?

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server pg-fin-01
System assigned managed identity on the vault
User assigned managed identities attached to the vault
contoso-backup-key - generated and rotated every 90 days by the Contoso security team
Backup Management Service app - Key Vault Crypto User

options.text: Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, but leave the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity disabled.
Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, and turn on the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity.
Under Encryption settings select Microsoft managed keys and turn on the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity, leaving the key lifecycle with the platform service.

Under Encryption settings select Customer Managed Keys and point the vault at the key in kv-contoso-crypto, but replace the Backup Management Service app's key read access with key read access for the vault's System Assigned Managed Identity.

explanation.correct: Two separate requirements are in play, and this option satisfies both. First, Contoso's requirement to own the encryption key is met by selecting Customer Managed Keys under the vault's Encryption settings and pointing the vault at contoso-backup-key in kv-contoso-crypto; with Microsoft managed keys the key stays under the platform service's control, so Contoso could not rotate or revoke it on its own authority. The key read for that arrangement is performed by the Backup Management Service app, which per the exhibit already holds Key Vault Crypto User on kv-contoso-crypto, so no permission change in the key vault is required. Second, access to backup and restore operations, including which workloads the vault may back up, is enforced through the managed identities associated with the vault. With the System Assigned Managed Identity disabled and no User Assigned Managed Identity attached, the vault currently has no identity carrying those grants. Because this vault serves a single team and is not shared, the System Assigned Managed Identity is the simplest choice to bring back.

perChoice.a: The encryption half is right, but the identity half is not. With the System Assigned Managed Identity disabled and no User Assigned Managed Identity attached, the vault has no managed identity at all, and it is through those identities that the vault's role-based access control, including the grants that decide which workloads it may back up, is enforced. Turning the System Assigned Managed Identity on is the simple fix for a vault used by a single team.
perChoice.c: Selecting Microsoft managed keys leaves the encryption key under the platform service's control, so Contoso cannot generate, rotate or revoke it on its own authority and the key-ownership part of the policy is not met. Turning on the identity only addresses the access side, and it also has to be paired with the customer-managed option.
perChoice.d: The key read for a vault that encrypts its data with a customer-managed key is performed by the Backup Management Service app, not by the vault's own managed identity; permissions given to the vault's identity in the key vault are not what makes that option work. Removing the app's access and giving it to the vault's identity instead takes away the access that the service actually needs, so backup jobs would fail with a key retrieval error.

body.stem:
You have a new Backup vault that Contoso is building for vaulted backups of a Blob container and a PostgreSQL flexible server, and you are writing the architecture section of the design document for it. Two functions in Contoso's operations runbook are attributed to the wrong principal, so you need to record, for each function below, which part of the architecture actually carries it out. The configuration in scope is shown below.

Match each function to the component that performs it.

rows: Blob container docs-prod; PostgreSQL flexible server pg-01

items.text: Azure Key Vault
Backup Management Service app
Managed identity of the vault
Identity that runs the backup operation
Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant

slots.label: Holds the secret material that Contoso's security team generates, rotates and revokes on its own
Performs the read of that secret material from the repository during an encryption operation
Carries the role grants that decide which workloads it is allowed to protect, and who may run backup and restore operations
Must already hold the Reader role on the source disk or database server before a protected instance can be created or updated
Where the recovery points accumulate; guests and other external principals have no direct route to it, and a compromised source environment cannot alter or wipe what is kept there

explanation.correct: Each slot describes one function of the vault's architecture, and each item names the part that actually carries that function out. The secret that Contoso creates, rotates and revokes is kept in Azure Key Vault, and the Backup Management Service app - not the vault's managed identity - is what reaches into Azure Key Vault to read it when the vault encrypts data with a customer-managed key. The role grants that limit which workloads the vault may back up and who may run backup and restore are enforced through the vault's managed identity. Whoever creates or updates a backup instance separately needs read permission on the source resource, for example the Reader role on the source disk or PostgreSQL server, and that grant belongs to the identity running the backup operation rather than to the vault's identity. Finally, the recovery points themselves are kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant that guests and external users cannot reach directly, which is why a compromised source environment cannot tamper with or wipe existing backups.

perChoice.keyvault: Fits the function of holding the secret material Contoso's security team generates, rotates and revokes: the Customer Managed Keys option on the vault points at a key stored in Azure Key Vault, and Contoso keeps control of that key's lifecycle.
perChoice.bmsapp: Fits the function of reading that secret material during an encryption operation: the Backup Management Service app is the actor that accesses Azure Key Vault for the key, and the managed identity of the Backup vault is explicitly not the actor, which is a common source of wrong runbook entries.
perChoice.vaultidentity: Fits the function of carrying the role grants: role-based access control on a Backup vault is enforced through the managed identities associated with it, and those grants can be tuned per workload, for example which Azure Disks or PostgreSQL servers the vault may back up.
perChoice.calleridentity: Fits the function of needing read permission on the source resource: the identity that creates or updates a backup instance must be able to read the source resources, for example through the Reader role on the source disk or PostgreSQL server, and this permission is separate from anything assigned to the vault's managed identity.
perChoice.isolatedstore: Fits the function of holding the recovery points with no direct route for guests: the vaulted backup data is stored in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, so external users and guests have no direct access to that storage or its contents and existing backups cannot be tampered with or deleted from a compromised source environment.

body.stem:
You have an Azure Backup vault named ops-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. It protects an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server, and the operations team keeps a runbook for the routine work carried out on this vault.

You need every task below to point at the part of the Azure Backup vault experience where that task is actually performed. Match each task to the correct place.

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server

items.text: Verify that this morning's scheduled runs finished and review the alerts raised for the protected server
Empty the list of protected items so that the vault itself can be removed afterwards
Run the final removal of an emptied vault and answer the prompt that appears
Set the name, region and storage redundancy for a brand-new vault before any workload is protected

slots.label: Resiliency blade
Backup Instances entry in the left navigation
Dashboard
Instance details section of the Basics tab

explanation.correct: The runbook tasks break down by where the vault experience actually carries them out. Scheduled runs and the alerts raised for protected workloads are viewed together in the Resiliency blade, which also offers the matching reporting for the vault's V2 workloads. The entries that still hold recovery points are cleared from the Backup Instances entry in the left navigation, because the portal refuses to remove a vault while such entries or policies remain. Once the vault holds nothing, the removal itself is started from its Dashboard by choosing Delete and answering the confirmation prompt with Yes. The vault's name, region and storage redundancy are captured in the Instance details section of the Basics tab when the vault is first created, and the redundancy cannot be changed once items are protected.

perChoice.a: This task belongs in the Resiliency blade. That is the single place where the backup jobs and the alerts for all V2 workloads of the vault can be watched, together with the matching reporting.
perChoice.b: This task belongs in the Backup Instances entry in the left navigation. That list holds the entries that must be removed first, otherwise the portal blocks the vault's removal with a message about existing backup instances or backup policies.
perChoice.c: This task belongs on the Dashboard. After the vault has been emptied, Delete is chosen on the dashboard and the confirmation prompt is answered with Yes, after which the portal returns to the New service menu.
perChoice.d: This task belongs in the Instance details section of the Basics tab. The Backup vault name, the Region and the Storage redundancy are collected there while the vault is being created, and the chosen redundancy is then frozen because it cannot be edited after items are protected.

body.stem:
You are creating a new Azure Backup vault named contoso-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription to hold recovery points for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server and for a Blob container. The security and operations teams have attached four guarantees to the sign-off for this vault, and each guarantee below is met by one characteristic of the Backup vault model. The team wants every guarantee recorded against the characteristic that delivers it.

Match each guarantee to the characteristic of the Backup vault that provides it.

rows: Copies held where no guest, outside partner or source-server intruder has a direct route into them
The copies must sit in a subscription and tenant that Contoso does not administer, so a compromised source environment cannot tamper with them or wipe them out.
Recovery that survives a compromise of the production environment and the servers holding the copies
Even if the production environment and the servers that hold the copies are both taken over, the recovery points must stay recoverable.
Different reach for different teams, down to the sources each may back up and the key stores each may use
One team may protect only the databases it owns, while another may additionally use the organization's own key stores for the keys that protect the copies.
One place to follow every job and alert, with matching reporting
Every job and every alert raised for the resources in the vault must be traceable from a single place, and reporting for the same must be available there too.

items.text: Data isolation
Enhanced capabilities to help secure backup data
Fine-grained control over which workloads the vault can access
Central monitoring of the V2 workloads

slots.label: Copies held where no guest, outside partner or source-server intruder has a direct route into them
Recovery that survives a compromise of the production environment and the servers holding the copies
Different reach for different teams, down to the sources each may back up and the key stores each may use
One place to follow every job and alert, with matching reporting

explanation.correct: Each guarantee lines up with exactly one characteristic of the Backup vault model. Data isolation puts the vaulted copies in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, so guests and outside partners have no direct route into them and a compromised source environment cannot tamper with or wipe them. The enhanced capabilities are what allow data to be recovered safely even when production and backup servers are both compromised. Fine-grained control over which workloads the vault can access is what separates the two teams, letting one be limited to the sources it owns while another additionally reaches the key stores used for encryption key management. Central monitoring of the V2 workloads is what puts backup jobs and alerts together in one place, with the matching reporting available in the Resiliency.

perChoice.i1: Data isolation is the characteristic that keeps the vaulted copies in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant where external users and guests have no direct access, so it is the one that satisfies the guarantee about copies staying out of reach.
perChoice.i2: These enhanced capabilities are what make it possible to recover data safely even when production and backup servers have been compromised, so this matches the guarantee about recovery surviving a compromise.
perChoice.i3: Fine-grained control over which workloads the vault can access is what grants different teams different reach, including which Azure Disks or PostgreSQL servers may be protected and which key stores are used for encryption key management.
perChoice.i4: Central monitoring of the V2 workloads is what allows all protected workloads to be watched from backup jobs through to alerts in one place, with matching reporting in the Resiliency.

Your team is standing up a new Azure Backup vault for the Contoso-prod subscription, and the platform team wants the deployment runbook to record exactly what an engineer does in the Azure portal to create it, in the order the portal expects. The specification the new vault has to meet is shown below.

You need the runbook to be correct, so match each action to its position in the sequence.

items.text: Type Backup vaults into the portal search box and open the Backup vaults entry listed under Services
On the Backup vaults page, select Add to open the creation experience
On the Basics tab, under Project details, select the subscription and use Create new to name the resource group
Under Instance details, type the Backup vault name and pick the Region
Choose the Storage redundancy, which cannot be adjusted once items are protected, and then select Review + create

slots.label: First action in the portal
Second action in the portal
Third action in the portal
Fourth action in the portal
Fifth action in the portal

explanation.correct: The portal takes the engineer through the service first, then the creation entry point, then the two sections of the Basics tab, and only then the final choice and submission: find Backup vaults in the search box and open it from Services, choose Add on that page, fill in Project details (subscription plus a resource group created with Create new), fill in Instance details (vault name and Region), and finish by choosing the Storage redundancy and selecting Review + create. The storage redundancy deliberately sits last of the settings because it is frozen once items are protected in the vault.

perChoice.act1: First position — the service is located through the portal search box and then opened from the list under Services, which is the entry point for everything that follows.
perChoice.act2: Second position — Add on the Backup vaults page opens the creation experience, where the tabs and fields for the new vault appear.
perChoice.act3: Third position — the Basics tab's Project details section takes the subscription and the resource group, and Create new is the link used there to create and name the resource group as part of this step.
perChoice.act4: Fourth position — Instance details on the Basics tab takes the Backup vault name and the Region, and it follows the project details in the same tab.
perChoice.act5: Fifth position — the Storage redundancy is the last value chosen, because it cannot be changed once items are protected, and Review + create is the button that submits the vault for creation.

body.stem:
You are building a new Azure Backup vault for the Contoso-prod subscription, and the design review recorded five obligations for the vault. The context for the new vault is shown below.

You need each obligation to be met by one of the configuration changes listed for dragging. Match each obligation to the configuration change that satisfies it.

rows: One Blob container (vaulted backup) and one Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server
Company's own copy of the blob data
Quarterly, run from the copies in the paired area with no failure declared in the primary area
Contoso's own security team generates, rotates and revokes the key material
Two platform teams administer the vault's grants; the vault will be deleted and rebuilt in June
Two storage volumes, one database instance, one Azure Key Vault

items.text: Create the Azure Backup vault with Locally redundant storage redundancy.
Create the Azure Backup vault with Geo-redundant storage redundancy and enable Cross Region Restore.
Create the Azure Backup vault with Geo-redundant storage redundancy and keep Cross Region Restore disabled.
Select Customer Managed Keys under Encryption settings on the Azure Backup vault.
Apply role assignments through the vault's managed identity so that it covers only the named workloads and the Azure Key Vault used for key management.

slots.label: The company's own copy of the data sits on-premises, recovery is carried out inside the vault's own area, and finance wants the smallest monthly Azure bill for the vault.

The company's primary copy is in Azure, and the team must be able to bring the database back from the copies held in the paired area on a scheduled date, even though nothing has failed in the primary area.

The primary copy of the protected data is in Azure, the stored recovery points have to survive the loss of an entire region, and the company does not want the extra storage rate that comes with the rehearsal capability.
The material that protects the data held in the vault has to be generated, stored, rotated and revoked by the company's own security team inside the company's own Azure Key Vault.
The vault has to be restricted to the storage volumes and database instances the security team signed off, plus the Azure Key Vault they chose.

explanation.correct: Each obligation maps to the vault configuration change that delivers it. An on-premises primary copy with same-area recovery and the smallest Azure bill points to Locally redundant storage redundancy chosen at creation, because that is the documented way to cut Azure storage spend when the original data is not held in Azure. Restoring from the copies held in the paired area on a scheduled date, while nothing has failed in the primary area, needs Geo-redundant storage plus Cross Region Restore turned on, because GRS replicates the backups to the paired region and Cross Region Restore allows restores from those secondary recovery points at any time without a declared outage. Surviving the loss of an entire region from an Azure-hosted primary copy while refusing the higher rate that the rehearsal capability brings points to Geo-redundant storage with Cross Region Restore left off, since a vault with Cross Region Restore enabled is billed automatically at RA-GRS rates. Generating, rotating and revoking the key material in the company's own Azure Key Vault points to the Customer Managed Keys option under Encryption settings, since the default Microsoft managed keys need no key-management effort by the customer. Finally, limiting the vault to the approved storage volumes, database instances and the chosen Azure Key Vault points to role assignments carried by the vault's managed identity, because RBAC on the vault can be tuned per workload, including which Azure Disks or PostgreSQL servers may be backed up and which Key Vaults are used for encryption key management.

perChoice.a: This belongs with the obligation about an on-premises primary copy, recovery inside the vault's own area, and the smallest Azure bill. When the original data is not kept in Azure, the guidance is to choose Locally redundant storage redundancy to cut Azure storage spend, and the redundancy level is set when the vault is created.
perChoice.b: This belongs with the obligation that recovery runs from the copies held in the paired area on a scheduled date while nothing has failed in the primary area. Geo-redundant storage replicates the backups to the paired Azure region, and enabling Cross Region Restore lets you restore from recovery points sitting in that secondary region at any time, with no outage declared in the primary region, which is what makes such drills possible.
perChoice.c: This belongs with the obligation that the recovery points must survive the loss of an entire region, that the primary copy is in Azure, and that the higher rate tied to the rehearsal capability must be avoided. Geo-redundant storage is the default when the primary copy is kept in Azure, and leaving Cross Region Restore off keeps the PostgreSQL backups on standard rates rather than the automatic RA-GRS rates applied when that capability is on.
perChoice.d: This belongs with the obligation that the company's own security team generates, rotates and revokes the key material inside the company's own Azure Key Vault. The Customer Managed Keys option under Encryption settings lets the organization bring its own key and manage its lifecycle, whereas the default Microsoft managed keys require no key-management effort.
perChoice.e: This belongs with the obligation that the vault is limited to the approved storage volumes and database instances plus the chosen Azure Key Vault. RBAC is enforced through the managed identities associated with the vault, and those role assignments can be tuned per workload, covering which Azure Disks or PostgreSQL servers may be backed up and which Key Vaults are used for encryption key management.

body.stem:
You are finalizing the access design for contoso-vault, a new Azure Backup vault in rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. It will hold vaulted backups of an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server named pg-fin, and Contoso brings its own encryption material for the vaulted data. The design decisions on record are shown below.

You need to record, for each requirement that came out of the security review, the scope in which the design grants or withholds the related access. Match each requirement to the correct scope.

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server named pg-fin
Runs as svc-backup-runner, the run-as identity of an automation account
Supplied by Contoso rather than generated by the service

items.text: Only engineers who hold the helpdesk role may start a restore of the stored recovery points.
The identity that runs the scheduled job must be able to read the server it protects.
Contoso's own encryption material, generated and rotated by its security team, must be usable by the service that protects the stored copies.
Guests and other external users must not be able to open the stored copies directly, even if the production environment is compromised.

slots.label: The Backup vault
The source resource
The Azure Key Vault
The Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant

explanation.correct: Each requirement lands on a different scope of the Backup vault model. Limiting restores to the helpdesk role is enforced by the role assignments made on the vault itself, because Backup vaults work with Azure RBAC and only the roles assigned there can reach backup and restore operations. Letting the scheduled job read the server it protects requires read permission on that source resource, held by the identity that creates or updates the backup instance rather than by the vault's managed identity. Using Contoso's own encryption material involves the Backup Management Service app reaching into Azure Key Vault to read the key, so the relevant permission is granted on the Key Vault that holds it, and the vault's own identity is not the actor. Finally, keeping guests and other external users away from the stored copies is achieved by the isolation of the backup storage in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where those external users have no direct route at all.

perChoice.i1: Belongs with the Backup vault: backup and restore operations on a Backup vault are gated by the role assignments made on that vault, so restricting who may start a restore is expressed by the vault's own access configuration.
perChoice.i2: Belongs with the source resource: whoever creates or updates a backup instance needs read permission on the resources that instance protects, and that grant sits on the protected server and belongs to the identity running the job, separately from any permissions held by the vault's managed identity.
perChoice.i3: Belongs with the Azure Key Vault: it is Azure Backup's own service that performs the read of a customer-supplied key, not the vault's managed identity, so the permission that makes the key usable is granted on the Key Vault where Contoso keeps it.
perChoice.i4: Belongs with the Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant: the vaulted copies are kept in Microsoft-managed storage, and guests and other external users have no direct route to that storage or its contents, so this access is withheld at that scope rather than granted anywhere in Contoso's own tenant.

body.stem: You have a Backup vault named pg-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. It holds recovery points for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server, and you have reviewed the configuration below. Leadership has decided that the stored recovery points must also survive the loss of the whole Azure region that hosts the vault, but the recovery points that already exist must not be destroyed. An engineer has asked what can be done on this vault to reach that goal. Which change should you make?

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server

body.statement: The change you should make is {{action}}.

options.text: Edit the storage redundancy of the existing vault in the Azure portal.
Edit the backup policy that is attached to the protected server in the existing vault.
Delete the backup instance that covers the protected server, then edit the storage redundancy of the existing vault.
Leave the storage redundancy of the existing vault unchanged, because that value is fixed when the vault is created.

explanation.correct: Storage redundancy is the one storage choice a Backup vault team makes, and it is made when the vault is created. The documentation is explicit that once items are protected in a vault, the redundancy level is locked, so a choice that turns out to be wrong cannot be edited in place afterwards. pg-vault already protects a PostgreSQL server, so its Locally redundant setting stays exactly as it is and cannot be edited in the portal, by editing the policy, or by clearing out backup instances. Because the recovery points that already exist must not be destroyed, the team keeps this vault as it is and reaches regional resilience by putting a vault with the redundancy it wants in place from the start and protecting the server there.

perChoice.action:a: The storage redundancy is not an editable property of a vault that already holds protected items: once items are protected the redundancy level is locked, so editing it in the portal does not turn this vault into a geographically redundant one.
perChoice.action:b: The backup policy controls when backups run and how long recovery points are kept; it does not control the redundancy of the vault's storage, so editing the policy leaves the Locally redundant setting in place.
perChoice.action:c: Removing the backup instance destroys the recovery points that already exist, and the redundancy stays locked once items have been protected, so this route both loses data and still fails to change the setting.

body.stem:
You have a Backup vault named fin-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription, and the configuration on record is shown below.

The operations team wants to watch the backup jobs and alerts raised for the protected workload from a single place, and finance has asked which charging model applies to the PostgreSQL recovery points while the vault is set up so that restores can be run from the paired Azure region at any time, without waiting for Microsoft to declare an outage in the primary region.

You need both answers recorded correctly. Where should the operations team watch backup jobs and alerts, and which charging model applies to the PostgreSQL backups while that setup is active?

rows: Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server (pg-fin)
Permitted at any time, without an outage declaration

body.statement: The operations team should watch the backup jobs and alerts for the protected workload in the {{slot1}}, and while the vault allows restores from the paired region on demand, the PostgreSQL backups it holds are charged at the {{slot2}}.

options.text: Resiliency blade
Backup Instances page
Backup Policies page
Encryption settings page
RA-GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups the vault holds
Standard GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups the vault holds
LRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups the vault holds
ZRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups the vault holds

explanation.correct: The Resiliency blade is the single place where the vault's V2 workloads can be watched from backup jobs up to alerts, with matching reporting. The behaviour described — restoring from the paired region at any time with no outage declared in the primary region — is the Cross Region Restore capability, and a vault with that capability enabled is billed automatically at RA-GRS rates for the PostgreSQL backups it holds, rather than at plain GRS rates.

perChoice.slot1:b: The Backup Instances page lists the protected items and their backup instances, and it is the place the portal guidance points engineers to when emptying a vault before deleting it; it is not the surface that shows the running jobs and alerts with matching reporting.
perChoice.slot1:c: Backup policies hold the schedule, retention and protection settings that drive backups; they are configuration to be read or edited, not the place where jobs and alerts for the protected workload are watched.
perChoice.slot1:d: Encryption settings only carries the vault's encryption configuration, such as the choice between Microsoft managed keys and a customer managed key, and provides no view of backup jobs or alerts.
perChoice.slot2:b: Plain GRS keeps the copy in the paired region sealed until Microsoft declares an outage in the primary region, so it is not the model applied while the vault can restore from that region on demand.
perChoice.slot2:c: LRS keeps copies only within the hosting region and is the cheaper option recommended when the primary copy of the data lives outside Azure; it does not match a vault whose PostgreSQL backups are replicated to the paired region and billed at RA-GRS.
perChoice.slot2:d: ZRS spreads copies across availability zones inside a single region and creates no paired-region copy at all, so it cannot be the model applied to a vault that restores from the paired region.

body.stem:
You are creating an Azure Backup vault named sec-vault in the Contoso-prod subscription to hold vaulted backup data for an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server named pg-fin. The security and audit teams have attached two conditions to the sign-off for this vault, and the conditions on record are shown below.

You need the vault to satisfy both conditions. Which statement correctly completes the description of the recovery points it holds?

exhibit.text:
Condition | Requirement recorded by the audit team
C1        | A full compromise of the production PostgreSQL server, including its administrator credentials, must not let the stored recovery points be changed or destroyed.
C2        | The audit evidence must name every party that can open the storage that holds the recovery points, and people outside Contoso who assist with restore drills must not be listed.

body.statement: The recovery points that the Backup vault holds for the protected workload are kept {{location}}, and {{compromise}}.

options.text: in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where guest accounts and external users have no direct route to the storage
in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, with access restricted by the vault's Azure RBAC assignments
in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, where principals with a backup role on the vault have direct reach to the storage
in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, with network rules leaving guest accounts and external users no direct route to the storage
they cannot be altered or wiped through the compromised environment
they can be altered or wiped through the compromised environment whenever a backup role is assigned on the vault
they are removed automatically once the source workload is compromised
they become read-only for anyone working from the compromised environment

explanation.correct: A Backup vault keeps the recovery points it accumulates in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, and guests and other external users have no direct route to that storage or its contents. Because the copy of the backup data lives outside the customer's own subscription and outside the reach of the workload's administrators, a compromised source environment cannot be used to alter or wipe the recovery points that already exist. Role-based control on the vault governs which principals may run backup and restore operations; it does not hand out a path into the storage itself.

perChoice.location:b: The recovery points are not stored in Contoso's own subscription and resource group; they are kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant. Role assignments on the vault control who may perform backup and restore operations; they are not a restriction applied to storage in the customer's own resource group.
perChoice.location:c: The location is right but the reach is wrong: holding one of the backup roles on the vault grants the ability to run backup and restore operations, not a direct path to the storage that holds the recovery points. Guests and other external users have no direct route to that storage at all.
perChoice.location:d: The recovery points are not held in Contoso's own subscription and resource group, and network rules are not what protects them. The isolation comes from the data being kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant that guests and external users cannot route to.
perChoice.compromise:b: Even when a principal holds a backup role on the vault, that role covers backup and restore operations rather than the stored recovery points themselves. Data isolation means a compromised source environment has no route to the storage, so existing backups cannot be changed or destroyed through it.
perChoice.compromise:c: Recovery points are not deleted automatically when the workload they protect is compromised. The isolation provided by the Backup vault model is what keeps existing backups intact and out of the compromised environment's reach.
perChoice.compromise:d: Recovery points do not turn read-only for a compromised environment; the guarantee is stronger than that. The data sits in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant with no direct route for the compromised source, so it can be neither modified nor deleted from there.

body.stem: You are updating the operations handbook for a Backup vault named store-vault in resource group rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription. The vault protects an Azure Blob container through vaulted backup, and the handbook must record accurately what the Contoso platform team is responsible for in terms of storage, and which storage decision sits with the team. You need that section to be correct. Which statement should you write?

options.text: sit in storage that Azure manages for you, and the redundancy set at creation is the only storage choice you make
sit in storage that Azure manages for you, and the redundancy set at creation can be changed later in the vault's storage settings
sit in a storage account that you create and administer, and the redundancy set at creation is the only storage choice you make
sit in a storage account that you create and administer, and the redundancy set at creation can be changed later in the vault's storage settings

explanation.correct: The Backup vault keeps its backup data in storage that the service manages on your behalf, so the Contoso platform team does not create, own or run a storage account for the recovery points. The one storage-related decision that remains theirs is the redundancy level chosen when the vault is created (Geo-redundant for store-vault). Because the vault already protects an Azure Blob container, that level is now locked and is not something the team can adjust afterwards.

perChoice.storage:b: The first half is right, but the second half is not: the redundancy level is fixed once items are protected in the vault, so it cannot be raised later, and the vault does not expose a storage setting for changing it.
perChoice.storage:c: The redundancy half is right, but the storage half is wrong: the vault's underlying storage is managed by the service for you, so there is no storage account for the team to create and administer.
perChoice.storage:d: Both halves are wrong: the recovery points live in storage that Azure manages for you rather than in a storage account the team owns, and the redundancy level chosen at creation cannot be changed once items are protected in the vault.

body.stem: You have an Azure Backup vault named audit-vault in resource group rg-continuity of the Contoso-prod subscription, and it protects an Azure Database for PostgreSQL - Flexible Server named pg-sales. The audit team has asked for a plain statement of where the recovery points produced for this vault are kept and which parties are able to get at that stored data, and you are writing that statement for the operations handbook. The configuration on record is shown below.
body.statement: The recovery points that this vault accumulates are kept in {{storageLocation}}.

options.text: a subscription and tenant managed by Microsoft, where guests and other external users have no route to the stored data
the Contoso-prod subscription and tenant, where guests and other external users have no route to the stored data
a subscription and tenant managed by Microsoft, where any principal holding Owner on Contoso-prod can read the stored data directly
the Contoso-prod subscription and tenant, where any principal holding Contributor on rg-continuity can read the stored data directly

explanation.correct: Azure Backup holds the backup data of a Backup vault in a subscription and tenant that Microsoft manages, and guests and other external users have no route into that storage or its contents. That isolation is what stops a compromised source environment from being used to alter or wipe the recovery points already stored. The vault resource itself lives in Contoso-prod, but the data it holds does not, so the statement that pairs the Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant with the absence of any route for guests and external users is the accurate one.

perChoice.storageLocation:b: The reachability half is right, but the location is wrong. Only the vault resource itself is created in the Contoso-prod subscription; the backup data it accumulates is kept in a subscription and tenant that Microsoft manages, not in Contoso's own subscription and tenant.
perChoice.storageLocation:c: The location is right, but the reachability is wrong. Because the data is isolated in a subscription and tenant that Microsoft manages, holding Owner on Contoso-prod does not hand an identity direct read access to the raw stored contents.
perChoice.storageLocation:d: Both halves are wrong. The stored data is not kept in the Contoso-prod subscription, and holding Contributor on rg-continuity does not give direct read access to the stored contents either, because the data sits outside that subscription and tenant.

body.stem:
Contoso is decommissioning the Azure Blob container that the vault blob-vault protects, and the platform team would like the vault to go away in the same change. The records compliance group has set a seven-year retrievability rule for the vaulted recovery points of that container, and no other copy of those points exists. The current situation is shown below.

You need an accurate statement for the change request. Which statement should you write?

rows: blob-vault, an Azure Backup vault in rg-backup of the Contoso-prod subscription
Blob container contoso-archive, protected through vaulted backup
12 points; the newest was taken three days ago
The points for this container must remain retrievable for seven years

body.statement: The change request should state that {{slot1}}.

options.text: the vault stays in place while the recovery points are still required, because removing a vault permanently destroys the backup items and the backup data the vault holds, and the removal cannot be reversed
the vault can be removed now, because the backup data is kept in the Microsoft-managed subscription and is retained independently of the vault
the vault can be removed now and re-created later in the same subscription, after which the earlier recovery points can be reached again
the vault can be removed now once the Blob container is decommissioned, because the recovery points are not tied to the protected workload

explanation.correct: Taking a vault out of service is a one-way operation: every backup item and all of the backup data for the protected servers are destroyed permanently, and the removal cannot be reversed. The vaulted recovery points for contoso-archive exist only inside blob-vault, so as long as the compliance rule keeps them retrievable for seven years, the vault has to stay where it is; removing it and later re-creating a vault with the same name would leave the container with no recovery points at all.

perChoice.slot1:b: This option mistakes the storage model for a retention guarantee. The vaulted data is kept in a Microsoft-managed subscription and tenant, which keeps it out of reach of guests and external users, but that isolation does not preserve the data once the vault itself is gone: removing the vault destroys the backup data it holds for good.
perChoice.slot1:c: A vault accumulates its own recovery points over time. A vault created later with the same name starts out with no recovery points of its own, so the earlier points cannot be reached again through it.
perChoice.slot1:d: The points are held by the vault, not by the protected workload. Once the Blob container is decommissioned the vault still holds them, and removing the vault destroys them, so the state of the workload itself has no bearing on whether they survive.
